newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore meets China Premier, witnesses business deals.
newsitem.headline: Gore meets China Premier, witnesses business deals.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Tuesday launched his first full day in China by ignoring a funding payment scandal and repairing ties by presiding over multi-million dollar aircraft sales and car ventures.

Gore witnessed a boom in U.S. sales and investment in China that overshadowed a scandal over alleged Chinese funding of U.S. Democratic Party politicians and marked important progress for U.S. companies that were passed over by Beijing when ties were strained.
Both sides appeared eager to paper over possible differences on issues such as human rights and the funding scandal to ensure an exchange of presidential visits over the next year.
"We had a very productive and energetic talk," Gore told reporters after meeting Premier Li Peng in the cavernous Great Hall of the People.

"The meetings today were very positive. Both sides have a desire to lend forward momentum...recognising areas where we agreed to disagree," said Gore, the most senior U.S. official to visit China since Beijing crushed student-led protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
China too appeared keen that disputes over human rights should not be allowed to overshadow business gains.
"There are in fact differences between China and the United States on some issues, including differences on human rights," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
"It would not be possible for there to be no differences between two such big nations with such contrasting cultures."
Gore did not specify whether he raised human rights.
Police in Beijing have told the tiny band of dissidents not to leave their homes during Gore's visit and have stepped up surveillance of their families, activists said.

In a sign of the rapidly improving ties between the world's top superpower and its fastest-growing Pacific neighbour, Gore and Li Peng witnessed the signings of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China.
Boeing Co signed a deal to sell five 777-200 jets worth $685 million to China's international carrier, Air China.

Analysts said the Chinese decision to buy the new-generation airliners was almost certainly based not only on aviation needs but on a thaw in ties since Sino-U.S. relations chilled in 1995 and early 1996 amid disputes over human rights and Taiwan.
The deal had been delayed by politics, said Ronald Woodard, president of Boeing Commercial Airplane Group.
Under the Boeing deal, three of the 777-200s are to be delivered to Air China by end-1998 and the other two in 1999.
Gore also witnessed the signing of a formal pact in which General Motors Corp launched a long-delayed joint venture with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp to build medium-sized cars.
Investment in the $1.57 billion motor project in Shanghai will be shared equally by the two corporations. The pact won initial go-ahead in 1995 but the final signing was subject to lengthy delays.
China's Li sounded a note of caution, reflecting China's concern about superpower politics and growing U.S. influence.
"China has high respect for the United States," Li said.

"We believe the United States, the biggest developed country in the world, should play a more positive role in international affairs," Li said. "The importance of our relations serves the interests of both peoples."

Officials dismissed reports that Gore hesitated to attend the signing ceremony because of allegations that China had tried to influence last year's U.S. presidential election by illegally funnelling cash to support President Bill Clinton's campaign.
"These agreements...are proof positive that there is greater economic cooperation between the United States and China," said Ginny Terzano, Gore's press secretary.
Gore's meetings with Beijing leaders aimed to strengthen a recent Sino-U.S. rapprochement, but his talks appeared likely to be darkened by the funding scandal.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
Under a third agreement signed on Tuesday, China will formally allow Washington to maintain a consulate in Hong Kong after 150 years of British rule ends at midnight on June 30.
